indie.title: They Dream in Gold
indie.author: Mai Sennaar
indie.publishing: Debut novel · SJP Lit / Zando, an independent publisher
indie.premise: A diasporic love story follows artistic ambition and the longing for belonging across continents.
indie.take: Our founding spotlight brings music, migration and an emerging literary voice together. Sennaar gives this shelf a connection to DSB’s music hall while showing that an independent publishing path can hold an expansive story.
indie.craft: an intergenerational narrative crossing places and relationships
indie.question: How can the desire to make art reshape the people and places someone calls home?

indie.title: Ode to Keisha
indie.author: Jamila Rowser; illustrated by Trinidad Escobar
indie.publishing: Independent comics · Black Josei Press edition
indie.premise: An autobiographical comic remembers a childhood friendship and its connection to Black girlhood, racism and sisterhood.
indie.take: A short comic can carry a lasting emotional argument. We include this because friendship is not a minor subject: it can help a child understand what recognition and shared identity feel like.
indie.craft: an autobiographical comic using both words and images
indie.question: How might a childhood friendship change the way someone understands their own identity?

indie.title: The Saddest Angriest Black Girl in Town
indie.author: Robyn Smith
indie.publishing: Originally self-published in 2016; later Black Josei Press edition
indie.premise: An autobiographical comic considers Blackness, mental health and life in a predominantly white Vermont town.
indie.take: Smith’s self-published beginnings make the independent path concrete. The short form offers a way into experiences of isolation without pretending that a single narrator can stand for every Black person in a white space.
indie.lens: isolation and the pressure of visibility
indie.craft: autobiographical comics joining graphite imagery and poetic language
indie.question: How can someone be watched closely and still feel that no one really sees them?

new.title: Kin
new.author: Tayari Jones
new.publishing: Selected recent release · first published February 24, 2026
new.premise: A novel explores two women’s friendship, family absence and the lives they build in the American South.
new.take: We chose this recent release for its attention to kinship beyond a simple family tree. It sits beside An American Marriage as another invitation to examine how intimate relationships carry social pressures.
new.lens: friendship and the meanings of kinship
new.craft: a character-centered narrative of intersecting lives
new.question: Who counts as family when a relationship is sustained by choice rather than only by birth?

new.title: Dream Count
new.author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
new.publishing: Selected recent novel · 2025 original; later editions vary
new.premise: Four women’s lives bring love, longing, choices and self-understanding into conversation.
new.take: This discovery belongs in the recent shelf rather than altering the fixed 100. It gives returning readers a way to follow an established author into another exploration of women’s lives and the stories they tell themselves.
new.lens: desire and the lives people imagine
new.question: What can a life someone imagined reveal about the life they actually live?

new.title: Good Dirt
new.author: Charmaine Wilkerson
new.publishing: Selected recent novel · 2025 original; 2026 paperback edition
new.premise: Family history, loss and the meaning of a treasured object connect the present to a longer inheritance.
new.take: Wilkerson offers a recent entry into a question running throughout our canon: how can an object carry a history that the people around it only partly understand? This is an editorial discovery, not a claim to list every new book.
new.craft: a family narrative moving across periods and perspectives
new.question: What would you need to know before deciding what an inherited object is worth?
